In summary, our research is concerned with
improving the quality of the exposure assessment of veterinary medicinal product residues.
the development of a set of realistic exposure scenarios for the environmental risk assessments of new veterinary medicinal product applications.
the development of models that can be used for the environmental risk assessments of veterinary medicines, taking the variability and uncertainty in the input parameters into account.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current models and data are inadequate to provide reliable predictions of environmental exposure concentrations.
there is still no reliable and validated model available to predict the exposure of fish to veterinary medicines in the aquatic environment.
there is no single best model for all situations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the models are useful tools to assess environmental risks, but the uncertainties associated with the model parameters and the assumptions made, should be taken into account.
the available data do not allow a clear conclusion on the applicability of models for the environmental fate of veterinary medicinal products.
the use of worst case scenarios in the exposure models for soil, surface water and groundwater is recommended for the environmental risk assessments of veterinary medicinal products.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of screening models for environmental risk assessment of medicines is only possible if the models have been properly validated against field data.
there is a need for a better understanding of the fate and behaviour of medicines in the environment.
it is impossible for a regulator to assess the contribution of every parameter in a model to the uncertainty in the prediction.
